whyThisMatters: AI makes risky shortcuts look safe — pasting code, customer data, or unapproved tools into a chatbot can expose what you were trying to protect.
rememberThis: If an AI tool isn't approved, don't feed it work data — check with IT first, and keep sensitive content local.

items.scenario: Paste proprietary source code into ChatGPT to help debug a function.
items.explanation: Code sent to public AI leaves your environment. Use local models or sanctioned internal AI tools instead.

items.scenario: Receive a voice message from your CEO requesting an urgent wire transfer. Call back on their known mobile number to verify.
items.explanation: Out-of-band verification (calling a known number) defeats voice cloning. Always verify unusual requests through a second channel.

items.scenario: Upload a customer PII spreadsheet to an AI tool to 'anonymize the data automatically'.
items.explanation: Sending PII to external AI violates data protection. Anonymize locally with approved scripts before any AI processing.

items.scenario: An email from IT asks you to click a link to 'verify your MFA setup' — the address bar shows the correct company domain.
items.explanation: If the domain is verified (check root domain, not subdomain) and you initiated the action, it's likely legitimate. Still, navigate manually when possible.

items.scenario: Use an AI meeting assistant that joins calls, transcribes, and summarizes — without checking if it's on the approved vendor list.
items.explanation: Unapproved AI bots can record sensitive discussions. Only use vetted tools with data processing agreements in place.

items.scenario: A colleague sends a Teams message with a QR code: 'Scan to confirm your voice ID for the new security system.'
items.explanation: Voice enrollment QR codes are a social engineering trap — they enroll the attacker's voice as yours. IT never enrolls via QR.

items.scenario: Generate a password using an AI prompt: 'Create a strong 16-char password for my bank account.'
items.explanation: Never generate real passwords via AI — the model/logs may retain them. Use a local password manager's generator instead.

items.scenario: A video call shows your manager's face and voice asking you to bypass approval for a vendor payment. You hang up and call them on their desk phone.
items.explanation: Deepfake video+audio on calls is real. Hanging up and calling a known number is the correct verification protocol.

items.scenario: Use the company-approved internal LLM (hosted on-prem) to draft a public-facing blog post about your project.
items.explanation: Approved internal models with data residency guarantees are safe for non-sensitive content. Still avoid feeding secrets.

items.scenario: Find a USB drive labeled 'Q3 Payroll Data' in the parking lot. Plug it into your workstation to see who it belongs to.
items.explanation: USB drops are a classic attack vector — auto-run malware, HID keystroke injection. Never plug in found media. Hand to IT.
